newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: ANALYSIS-MARKET NEEDS PRIVATE PENSION BOOST-EXPERTS.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSIS-MARKET NEEDS PRIVATE PENSION BOOST-EXPERTS.

text.p: Lithuania's financial markets need private pension funds to attract hesitant local investors and mobilise national savings, analysts said on Friday.
Currently there are no private pension funds in Lithuania but work in parliament on drawing up the necessary legislation is going on at the moment.
"Maybe a new law could go into effect next year," Kestutis Glaveckas, vice-chairman of parliament's finance committee, told Reuters. "Realistically, a law could be passed this autumn."
"The financial market needs private pension funds," Glaveckas said.
Parliament is expected to take up pension legislation in the third week of June, Glaveckas said.
Currently Lithuania has a pay-as-you-earn pension system, which some say is difficult to maintain and should slowly be moved toward a fully-funded system.

"Probably it's true about any country that they (pay-as-you-earn systems) are not sustainable," said Elena Leontjeva, president of the Lithauanian Free Market Institute, which has pushed hard for pension reform.
Local International Monetary Fund (IMF) representative Domenico Fanizza also backed the formation of private pension funds and said it would have a positive effect on local capital markets.
"They should gradually introduce elements of a private system," he said. "This cannot be done immediately, it has to be done in a gradual way."
"It could favour the mobilisation of savings," Fanizza said. "That's the experience in most countries.
Employees must currently contribute one percent of salaries to the state SODRA fund while employers contribute 30 percent.
On top of the 33 percent personal income tax, Leontjeva said the tax burden was too high and resulted in tax evasion.
"The total tax burden is over 60 percent for labour," Leontjeva said.

"As a first step, we are suggesting a limit to the income that should be paid to SODRA as well as tax deductibility," Leontjeva said. "There is no tax deductibility now, so you can save but you must save from your taxed income," Leontjeva said.
"I want to pay into private funds but I am obliged to contribute to the state fund," said Margarita Starkevichiute, an analyst at the central securities depository.
"Of course the government says I can do it voluntarily but I don't have the money to do that," she added.
She said that if pension funds were started, they would be viewed as a safe way to invest and save in a country where many people do not trust banks.
A recent poll in newspaper Respublika showed that 84 percent of those polled did not trust commercial banks.
"Deposits in banks amount to $1.2 billion," Starkevichiute said. "I think an additional $1.2 billion is not being used because people are afraid of devaluation, a banking crisis or banking scandals."
